anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite Anomaly Definition: The database simultaneously suffers from accelerated accumulation of obsolete MVCC row versions and saturation of the underlying storage-subsystem’s read/write throughput. The version store keeps expanding while the physical devices that must hold, read, and clean those extra pages are already at or beyond their performance envelope.

Combined Observable Phenomena: Administrators will notice rapidly growing table and index sizes, soaring obsolete-to-live row ratios, and autovacuum/cleaner workers that run constantly yet make little progress. At the same time, I/O wait events dominate wait-class statistics; average and p-99 latencies for data-file, log, and temp-space operations rise sharply; queue depths remain full; and overall transaction response times elongate even though CPU utilization is modest. Sequential scans and index probes both touch many more pages because of bloat, compounding physical I/O. Planner misestimates lead to poor plans, while checkpoints, WAL flushes, and batch jobs overrun their windows due to throttled bandwidth. Alerts may escalate for near-term transaction-ID wraparound, version-store exhaustion, or log flush timeouts.

Causal Interaction: Excessive update/delete churn produces large numbers of dead tuples that background cleanup workers must remove. Each cleanup cycle issues additional reads and writes, inflating I/O demand. When the storage layer is already throughput-constrained, these maintenance I/Os contend with foreground queries and deferred writes, slowing both application workload and cleanup itself. The slowdown lets even more obsolete versions pile up, further bloating on-disk structures and increasing every future I/O operation’s cost. This positive feedback loop—version bloat increasing I/O volume, and I/O saturation throttling bloat removal—drives the system into a self-reinforcing degradation spiral that jeopardizes performance, space availability, and transactional safety.

entry.official_definition: Sets the interval between optional checks that the client is still connected while running queries.
entry.trigger_condition: During a long-running query, PostgreSQL polls the socket at this interval and can detect a closed connection sooner.
entry.workload_impact: Long-running queries can be aborted sooner after the kernel reports that the client connection is closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, disabling connection checks.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
